data.reasoning: Both models reviewed identical files (PKGBUILD, .SRCINFO, LICENSE, .gitignore, REUSE.toml) and reached the same substantive conclusion: the package is a standard AUR VCS package with no malicious behavior. The PKGBUILD sources from the legitimate upstream GitHub repository (https://github.com/jawah/qh3), uses standard VCS packaging patterns (SKIP checksums, git source), and contains only routine build/install operations. The maintainer email obfuscation is in a comment and not executed. The only disagreement was caused by a transient API error (HTTP 400) in the qwen model's second review of LICENSE, which incorrectly escalated the overall verdict to 'inconclusive' despite the first LICENSE review succeeding with SAFE status.
data.disagreement_analysis: The disagreement is artificial - caused by a tool/API error in qwen3-235b, not by substantive analytical differences. Both models independently assessed all files as safe with equivalent reasoning. The qwen model actually reviewed LICENSE successfully on first attempt (SAFE), then encountered an API failure on a duplicate review, which the tool incorrectly treated as an inconclusive file verdict overriding the successful assessment.
coverage_issues: qwen3-235b experienced API error (HTTP 400 BadRequestError) on duplicate LICENSE review, causing false inconclusive status
Neither model attempted source fetch to verify upstream repository contents, though this is acceptable for -git packages where the PKGBUILD itself contains no injection
learnings: Tool should not allow a failed duplicate file review to override a successful earlier review of the same file - implement deduplication or fallback to first successful assessment
Transient API errors should not escalate package verdict to 'inconclusive' when the file was already successfully assessed - distinguish between 'never reviewed' and 'review failed after success'

For VCS packages, models correctly focus on PKGBUILD functions rather than attempting to fetch upstream source - this behavior should be preserved as it matches the threat model (injection in packaging, not upstream application behavior)
